ety.text: From Middle English me, from Old English mē (“me”, originally dative, but later also accusative, supplanting accusative mec), from Proto-West Germanic *miʀ, from Proto-Germanic *miz (“me”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁me- (“me”). Cognate with Scots me, North Frisian me, Saterland Frisian mie, Dutch me, mij, Low German mi, German mir (dative only), Icelandic mér (also still dative), Latin mē, Ancient Greek μέ (mé), ἐμέ (emé), Sanskrit मा (mā), all meaning “me”.

ety.text: From Middle English me, an unstressed phonetic reduction of men, man (pronouns; q. v.). Compare German man (“one, you”, indefinite pronoun).

senses.d: As the object (direct or indirect) of a verb.
Myself; as a reflexive direct object of a verb.
ex: And I awoke, and found me here.

senses.d: Myself; as a reflexive indirect object of a verb; the ethical dative.
ex: When I get to college, I'm gonna get me a white Nissan Sentra.

senses.d: As the object of a preposition.
Used in isolation or apposition, or (sometimes proscribed) as the complement of the copula (be).
ex: Who did this? —Me. I did it. (or:) It was me. I did it.)

senses.d: As the subject of a verb.
ex: Me and my friends played a game.
[It was] literally all me and my astrophysicist colleagues could talk about.

senses.d: As the subject of a verb. Sometimes used to indicate or imitate limited English fluency.
ex: Well he said me mustn’t eat ’nanas cause ’nanas would make me sick.
Whoa! That was about the coolest thing ever! Me gotta see that again.

senses.d: Would be the subject of a copula in standard English, though the copula is omitted; used to indicate or imitate limited English fluency.
ex: May opened the door, and a huge Indian walked into the room. “Me Bear Tracks,” he said. “Me hungry.”

senses.d: The self or personality of the speaker, especially their authentic self.
The solfeggio syllable used to indicate the flat of the third note of a major scale.
Indefinite pronoun (usually singular); one; you; they; someone.
